overview.text: Meiosis is a specialized nuclear division in eukaryotes that reduces chromosome sets from two (diploid) to one (haploid), producing cells needed for sexual reproduction. In animals, those cells develop into egg or sperm gametes, which can fuse at fertilization to restore diploidy. After one round of DNA copying, meiosis has two divisions: homologous chromosome pairs separate in meiosis I, then sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, usually yielding four haploid cells. During prophase I, paired chromosomes exchange DNA, and their random orientation also reshuffles inherited combinations. These processes make meiotic products genetically different and distinguish meiosis from mitosis, which preserves chromosome-set number in its daughter nuclei.

key_facts.text: Meiosis begins after one round of DNA replication; its first division separates homologous chromosome pairs and reduces the number of chromosome sets.
In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair, and non-sister chromatids can exchange chromosome segments—a process called crossing over.
The random alignment of homologous pairs in meiosis I is called independent assortment and contributes to genetic variation.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids; the process typically ends with four haploid cells, though their fate differs among organisms.
Crossing over exchanges DNA between paired homologous chromosomes and creates new combinations of alleles in egg or sperm cells.
